warn.nonNumeric: {name}: {count} cells are not numbers and count as missing.

describe.heading: Descriptive statistics
describe.pick: Tick one or more variables above to describe them.
describe.cvNote: CV is shown only for a variable on a ratio scale (tick "Ratio scale" in the variable dialog) with a positive mean.
describe.quartileNote: Q1 and Q3 (QUARTILE.EXC) need at least 3 values.
describe.groupId: {name} looks like an ID column, so it cannot be used to form groups. Untick it or change it in the variable dialog.
describe.firstGroupOnly: Only the first ticked nominal or ordinal variable ({name}) is used to form groups.
describe.twoOnly: Only the first two ticked nominal or ordinal variables are cross-tabulated.
describe.interp.summary: {name}: {n} values were used{missing}. The mean is {mean}{unit} and the standard deviation is {sd}{unit}, so a typical value lies about {sd}{unit} away from the mean. The values run from {min} to {max}{unit}.
describe.interp.quartiles: Half of the values are at or below the median of {median}{unit}; the middle half lies between Q1 = {q1} and Q3 = {q3}.
describe.interp.skewRight: The skewness of {skew} is positive: the distribution has a longer tail towards high values.
describe.interp.skewLeft: The skewness of {skew} is negative: the distribution has a longer tail towards low values.
describe.interp.skewNone: The skewness of {skew} is close to zero: the distribution is roughly symmetric.
describe.interp.cv: The coefficient of variation is {cv}%: the standard deviation is {cv}% of the mean.
describe.interp.ci: The {level}% confidence interval for the mean runs from {lower} to {upper}{unit}. An interval built this way contains the population mean in {level}% of samples.
describe.ciUnreliable: † n·p̂ or n·(1 − p̂) is below 5 for this category, so its interval is unreliable; more data is needed.
describe.interp.freq: The table counts how often each category of {name} occurs among {n} valid values{missing}. The most frequent category is {top} ({count} values, {pct}%). The cumulative % adds up the shares from the top row down.
describe.interp.freqCi: For each category, the {level}% confidence interval (Wald) estimates the share of that category in the population.
describe.interp.cont: The counts table shows how many cases fall in each combination of {row} and {col}, out of {n} cases with both values{missing}. Row % shows how {col} is spread within each category of {row}; column % shows how {row} is spread within each category of {col}.
describe.noOutliers: No values lie outside the fences.
describe.outlierAdvice: Investigate these values; do not delete them automatically. If they change the conclusion, report the results with and without them.
chart.swNA: Shapiro–Wilk needs 3 to 5000 values that are not all equal.
chart.swCaption: A p-value above 0.05 does not prove normality. Judge from the histogram and the Q-Q plot; with n ≥ 30 per group the methods here are robust.
ss.heading: Sample size
ss.sigmaHelp: From an earlier study, or paste 10–15 pilot values below to compute it.
ss.pHelp: Use 50% if you have no estimate; it gives the largest n.
ss.invalid: Enter a positive value for every input (p between 0 and 100%).
ss.interp.mean: With {level}% confidence, a standard deviation of {sigma}{unit} and a margin of error of ±{e}{unit}, each group needs at least {n} cases (always rounded up). With {groups} group(s), plan for {total} cases in total.
ss.interp.prop: With {level}% confidence, an expected proportion of {p}% and a margin of error of ±{e} percentage points, each group needs at least {n} cases (always rounded up). With {groups} group(s), plan for {total} cases in total.
ss.minMean: At least 30 per group when comparing means.
ss.minProp: For proportions, n·p ≥ 5 and n·(1 − p) ≥ 5 in every group.
ss.minChi: For a chi-square test, an expected count of at least 5 in every cell.
ss.belowMean: This is below 30 per group: plan for at least 30.
ss.belowProp: n·p or n·(1 − p) would be below 5: plan for a larger sample.
tests.manualIntro: Inputs and intermediate values, unrounded (6 significant figures). Differences in the third decimal place usually come from rounding during a hand calculation.
tests.interp.reject: p {p} is below α = {alpha}, so the null hypothesis ({h0}) is rejected.
tests.interp.noReject: p {p} is not below α = {alpha}, so the null hypothesis ({h0}) is not rejected.
tests.pick: Tick variables above; the test is chosen from what you tick.
tests.unsupported: This combination of ticked variables has no test here. Supported combinations: 1 metric (one-sample t-test); 1 nominal or ordinal (one-proportion z-test with 2 categories, chi-square goodness-of-fit with 3 or more); 1 metric + 1 nominal (two-sample t-test with 2 groups, one-way ANOVA with 3 or more); 2 metric (paired t-test); 2 nominal (two-proportion z-test and chi-square test of independence).
tests.ordinalNote: {name} is ordinal. This test needs a nominal variable: if its categories can be treated as unordered, change its level to nominal in the variable dialog.
tests.oneCategory: {name} has fewer than two categories among the usable rows, so there is nothing to compare.
tests.tooFew: Too few usable values for this test (at least 2 per group are needed).
tests.condFail: not met — the normal approximation is unreliable; more data is needed
tests.n30: With n ≥ 30 per group the t-test is robust to non-normality; with smaller groups, look closely at the Q-Q plots.
tests.sdRatio: SD ratio (larger / smaller): {ratio}. A ratio below 2 is usually fine.
os.title: One-sample t-test
os.enterValue: Enter the test value μ₀ (for example a target) to run the test.
os.h0: The population mean of {var} is **equal to** {mu0}{unit}.
os.h1.two-sided: The population mean of {var} is **not equal to** {mu0}{unit}.
os.h1.greater: The population mean of {var} is **greater than** {mu0}{unit}.
os.h1.less: The population mean of {var} is **less than** {mu0}{unit}.
os.interp: The test compares the sample mean {mean}{unit} with the test value {mu0}{unit}. The difference of {diff}{unit} is t = {t} standard errors from zero (SE = s/√n = {se}); with df = {df}, the {tail} p-value is {p}.
op.title: One-proportion z-test
op.h0: The population share of {var} = {cat} is **equal to** {p0}%.
op.h1.two-sided: The population share of {var} = {cat} is **not equal to** {p0}%.
op.h1.greater: The population share of {var} = {cat} is **greater than** {p0}%.
op.h1.less: The population share of {var} = {cat} is **less than** {p0}%.
op.interp: {x} of {n} cases are {cat}, so p̂ = {phat}%. Under H₀ the standard error is √(p₀(1 − p₀)/n) = {se}, giving z = {z} and a {tail} p-value of {p}. The confidence interval uses √(p̂(1 − p̂)/n) instead (Wald interval).
ws.title: Two-sample t-test (Welch)
ws.h0: There is **no difference** between {g1} and {g2} in the population mean of {var}.
ws.h1.two-sided: There **is a difference** between {g1} and {g2} in the population mean of {var}.
ws.h1.greater: The population mean of {var} is **higher** in {g1} than in {g2}.
ws.h1.less: The population mean of {var} is **lower** in {g1} than in {g2}.
ws.h0short: the two population means are equal
ws.interp: The difference in means, {g1} − {g2} = {diff}{unit}, is t = {t} standard errors from zero (SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) = {se}). With the Welch–Satterthwaite df = {df}, the {tail} p-value is {p}. Equal variances are not assumed.
pt.title: Paired t-test
pt.note: This assumes each row is the same unit measured twice. To see whether two measures move together, use the Correlation tab.
pt.h1.two-sided: The population mean difference {after} − {before} is **not zero**.
pt.h1.greater: The population mean difference {after} − {before} is **greater than zero**.
pt.h1.less: The population mean difference {after} − {before} is **less than zero**.
pt.interp: Across {n} pairs, the mean difference d̄ = {d}{unit} is t = {t} standard errors from zero (SE = s_d/√n = {se}); with df = {df}, the {tail} p-value is {p}.
tp.title: Two-proportion z-test
tp.h0: The population share of {outcome} = {cat} is **the same** in {g1} and {g2}.
tp.h1.two-sided: The population share of {outcome} = {cat} **differs** between {g1} and {g2}.
tp.h1.greater: The population share of {outcome} = {cat} is **higher** in {g1} than in {g2}.
tp.h1.less: The population share of {outcome} = {cat} is **lower** in {g1} than in {g2}.
tp.h0short: the two population shares are equal
tp.interp: The pooled share p̄ = {pooled}% gives a standard error under H₀ of √(p̄(1 − p̄)(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)) = {se}; the difference of {diff} percentage points is z = {z}, with a {tail} p-value of {p}. The confidence interval uses the unpooled standard error.
tp.cond: At least 5 successes and 5 failures in every group: {verdict}.
tp.z2: z² = {z2} equals χ² = {chi2} for a 2 × 2 table (two-sided test).
tp.countsInvalid: Enter whole numbers with 0 ≤ successes ≤ total and total ≥ 1 in both groups.
an.title: One-way ANOVA
an.h0: The population mean of {var} is **the same** in all {k} groups of {group}.
an.h1: **At least one** group of {group} has a different population mean of {var}.
an.interp: F = MS between / MS within = {f}. With df = ({df1}, {df2}), the p-value (the area to the right of F) is {p}.
an.tukeyInterp: Each row compares two groups (first − second). The p-values and the {level}% confidence intervals are adjusted for making {m} comparisons at once (studentized range with k = {k} and df = {df}; q crit = {qcrit}). A pair with p below α = {alpha} has an interval that does not include 0.
an.tukeyNotSig: The ANOVA itself is not significant at α = {alpha}, so pairwise differences are usually not interpreted.
an.leveneInterp: Levene's test checks whether the group variances differ (H₀: equal variances). p {p}: {verdict}
an.leveneDiffer: the spreads differ more than chance alone would explain.
an.leveneSame: no evidence that the spreads differ.
cs.title: Chi-square test of independence
cs.smallCells: {count} cell(s) have an expected count below 5: {cells}. Every cell should have at least 5; consider merging categories.
cs.interp: Each expected count is row total × column total / N. χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = {chi2} with df = (r − 1)(c − 1) = {df}; the p-value (the area to the right of χ²) is {p}. No continuity (Yates) correction is applied.
cs.tableHelp: Paste a table of counts from Excel: the first row holds the column categories, the first column the row categories.
cs.tableInvalid: The table needs at least 2 rows and 2 columns of whole-number counts, with labels in the first row and column.
gof.title: Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
gof.sumWarn: The shares add up to {sum}%; they must add up to 100%.
gof.h0: The distribution of {var} **matches** the expected shares.
gof.h1: The distribution of {var} **does not match** the expected shares.
gof.h0short: the distribution matches the expected shares
gof.interp: Expected count = expected share × n (n = {n}). χ² = Σ(O − E)²/E = {chi2} with df = k − 1 = {df}; the p-value is {p}.
cor.title: Pearson correlation
cor.pick: Tick two or more metric variables above.
cor.metricOnly: Only metric variables are used for correlation; the other ticked variables are ignored.
cor.h0: There is **no linear correlation** between {x} and {y} in the population (ρ = 0).
cor.h1: There **is a linear correlation** between {x} and {y} in the population (ρ ≠ 0).
cor.interp: r = {r} for {x} and {y} (n = {n}). The sign shows the direction of the linear relationship and the closer |r| is to 1, the closer the points lie to a straight line. The test of ρ = 0 uses t = r√(n − 2)/√(1 − r²) = {t} with df = {df}; the two-sided p-value is {p}.
cor.causation: Correlation is not causation: a correlation between two variables does not show that one causes the other.
reg.title: Simple linear regression
reg.pick: Choose a dependent and an independent variable above (both metric).
reg.equationMeaning: For each additional {xunit} of {x}, the predicted {y} is {b1abs} {yunit} {direction}. When {x} is 0, the predicted {y} is {b0}{yunitSuffix} (this only has a meaning if 0 lies within the observed range of {x}).
reg.h0: The population slope of {x} is **zero**: {x} does not help to predict {y} linearly.
reg.h1: The population slope of {x} is **not zero**.
reg.summaryInterp: R = {R} is the correlation between {x} and {y}. R² = {R2}: {pct}% of the variation in {y} is accounted for by the straight line on {x}. The standard error of the estimate, {see}{yunit}, is the typical distance of an observed {y} from the line.
reg.anovaInterp: The ANOVA tests whether the line explains any variation in {y}: F = {f} with df = (1, {df}), p {p}. In simple regression this p-value equals the p-value of the slope.
reg.coefInterp: B is the estimated intercept and slope. Each t = B / SE tests whether the population value is zero (df = {df}); the {level}% confidence interval gives the range of plausible population values.
reg.residualNote: Residuals should scatter randomly around 0 with an even spread; a curve or a funnel shape suggests the straight line does not fit well.
reg.extrapolation: {x0} lies outside the observed range of {x} ({min} to {max}). This is extrapolation: the line may not hold there.
reg.sameVar: The dependent and independent variable must be different.

guides.title: Method guides
guides.intro: One page per method, built from the app's own templates and filled with results from the example datasets. Print them, or save them as PDF from the print dialog.
guides.question: Question
guides.conclusionText: The app stops at the statistical decision. Write the business conclusion and any recommendation yourself, in the context of your data, and do not claim cause and effect from these results.
g.as.ciMean: The values are a random sample from the population; the distribution is roughly normal, or n ≥ 30 (look at the histogram and the Q-Q plot).
g.as.ciProp: n·p̂ ≥ 5 and n·(1 − p̂) ≥ 5 for the category; otherwise the interval is unreliable and more data is needed.
g.as.welch: Two independent groups; roughly normal within each group or n ≥ 30 per group (Q-Q plot per group). Equal variances are not needed (Welch).
g.as.paired: Each row is the same unit measured twice; the differences are roughly normal, or n ≥ 30.
g.as.twoProp: Independent groups; at least 5 successes and 5 failures in each group.
g.as.anova: Independent groups; roughly normal within each group or n ≥ 30 per group; comparable spread (largest / smallest SD below 2, Levene's test).
g.as.chi: Each case is counted once; the expected count is at least 5 in every cell (merge categories otherwise). No Yates correction.
g.as.gof: Each case is counted once; the expected count is at least 5 in every category; the expected shares add up to 100%.
g.as.reg: The relationship is roughly linear (scatter plot); the residuals scatter evenly around 0 (residual plot); do not predict outside the observed range of X.
g.as.outliers: Look for outliers in the box plot; investigate them, do not delete them automatically.
